name: Eminence
lede: Eminence is a deep purple, a dictionary name from the Maerz and Paul era whose meaning of rank and distinction is the only story our books support.

sections.title: A deep purple with a title
sections.body:
Eminence appears in Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930 and in the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, where it falls in block 224 and sits about 3.2 units from the block called deep purple [1]. The books in our collection do not explain the choice of name, so the origin is undocumented [1][2].

The word itself is about rank. Pre-eminence marks distinction in the books, and the color scarlet is described as an indication of royalty or pre-eminence [3]. No source here says the color was named with that sense in mind [3].

sections.title: Eminence grise
sections.body:
The most famous eminence in color is the grey one. Paterson's dictionary explains *éminence grise* as the power behind the throne, a name that began with Cardinal Richelieu's secretary, Père Joseph, who stayed in the background [4]. Jarman's *Chroma* repeats the phrase when writing about grey clothing [5]. Gérôme painted *L'Éminence grise* in 1873, now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston [6].

So in color history Eminence is a word for hidden power, and the grey sense belongs to that phrase, not to this purple [4][5][6].

sections.title: Where it sits
sections.body: Eminence is darker and bluer than [[purple]], and richer than [[orchid]], near [[heliotrope]] on the violet side [1]. Its Munsell notation is about 4.9P 3.1/11.0, a dark, strongly chromatic purple [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our painting archive is very thin here: within the strict match, only one of 23,781 paintings carries this color (0.00 per cent), as photographed [7]. The books we have do not date a single pigment to this exact swatch, so we do not guess [7][1].

In printed English, the word eminence peaks in the 1800s in Google Books [7]. That curve shows the vocabulary in general, not this color or the paint.
